name: Thunder-Magnus
description: Thunder-Magnus is a gas giant whose atmosphere produces electrical storms on a scale that beggars description. Lightning bolts thousands of kilometers long arc between cloud layers, illuminating the atmosphere in strobing flashes that are visible from neighboring worlds. The planet-spanning hurricane at the southern pole generates a continuous electromagnetic roar that has been detected by receivers across the sector. Dark amber and crimson bands alternate with zones of pale yellow, the colors shifting as chemical reactions driven by the lightning alter the atmospheric composition in real time.

The thunder from the electrical storms propagates through the dense atmosphere as infrasonic waves, vibrations that atmospheric probes register as a continuous seismic event. The magnetic field is enormously powerful and unstable, flipping polarity at irregular intervals that trigger global lightning cascades. The planet seems to exist in a state of perpetual electrical crisis, each storm feeding the next in a chain reaction that has been running since the world formed.

Large atmospheric fauna have been observed riding the storm fronts, organisms that appear to metabolize the electrical energy directly. These creatures, some estimated at over a kilometer in length, are translucent and visible primarily by the lightning that plays across their bodies. An ancient navigation beacon in stable orbit broadcasts coordinates and atmospheric data, its design suggesting construction by an advanced civilization that studied or perhaps cultivated the storm-fauna.

Thunder-Magnus presents extraordinary opportunities in both energy harvesting and xenobiology. The storm-fauna represent a form of life utterly unlike anything in the known biological catalogue, organisms that eat lightning and grow to mountainous proportions. The exotic matter traces in the deep atmosphere add further incentive. But the electromagnetic environment destroys unshielded electronics within minutes, and the lightning has already claimed several exploration vessels that ventured too deep into the cloud layers.
